newsitem.title: PERU: Japan learns lesson on tough diplomacy in Peru.
newsitem.headline: Japan learns lesson on tough diplomacy in Peru.

text.p: Japan, under fire in the past for giving in too easily to hostage takers, has been taught a lesson in old-style samurai toughness from Peruvian president Alberto Fujimori, whose parents left a Japanese village early this century.

Initially critical of Lima's hard line, Tokyo was by Sunday throwing its full weight behind Fujimori's tough stance toward negotiating with the rebels over the fate of the roughly 340 hostages held in the Japanese embassy residence in Lima.
Japanese foreign minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who had been here since Thursday for a round of crisis diplomacy, flew home Sunday apparently empty-handed and sidelined.

After adopting a low profile through much of his visit, Ikeda finally endorsed Fujimori's stern Saturday night lecture to the guerrillas to lay down their weapons and release the hostages to avoid bloodshed. In Tokyo, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto also backed Fujimori.

During Ikeda's four days here as Japan's point man in the efforts to resolve the the siege of the Japanese residence by the Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), Tokyo's attitude appeared to have moved from initial dovishness closer to Lima's hard line.
Last Friday, chief government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said that the two coutries were "far apart in ideas" on how to resolve the crisis.
But by the weekend, Hashimoto was echoing Fujimori's hard line taken in the televised speech to the MRTA -- a message so tough it had some Peruvian citizens fearing a bloodbath was imminent.
"It is the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's turn to respond. Japan supports President Fujimori's televised message to the nation," Hashimoto said on Sunday.

Japanese officials, stung by suggestions that they have been sidelined in the Lima crisis, defended their low-key diplomacy pointing out that Ikeda left Lima with both countries agreed on a course of action to deal with the rebels.
They also said that Japan was no longer an innocent abroad in the harsh world of international terrorism.

"Remember that we have signed a G-7 (Group of Seven Industrialised Nations) summit communique against terrorism," one official said. "We're simply not as naive as we once may have tought to have been."
The lessons of loss of innocence started last year in Japan with its own home-grown guerrilla movement, a doomsday cult that wanted to bring down the government with a poison gas attack.
In January 1995, the Kobe earthquake that killed about 5,000 people had already started to shake Japan's faith in its old way of dealing with crises.
The Japanese government was criticised both at home and abroad for its bungling of both the earthquake and the poison gas attack. Critics said it was slow to act and indecisive.
Japan went into the Lima hostage drama still shaky from the kidnapping in August of a top Japanese business executive in the Mexican border town of Tijuana.
It was widely believed that the victim's employer Sanyo Electric paid the $2 million ransom requested by the kidnappers to secure his release.
Many people expected Japan to use the same checkbook tactics in dealing with the Peruvian rebels.
But Japan, under its new sword-fighting prime minister Hashimoto, may have learned its lesson from the Tijuana incident.
Over the past five days Japanese newspapers have portrayed the Lima siege as a test of Hashimoto's ability to handle a major crisis and Tokyo's commitment to the anti-terrorism summit declarations.

By throwing its weight behind Fujimori's hard line and shaking off perceptions that it may either use its purse or its cultural ties with Japanese descendent Fujimori, Japan may gain greater international credibility to back up the influence it already wields as the world's largest aid donor.

"I think it was great -- an aid donor and an aid recipient was able to truly work together for a common purpose. People don't like to believe it, but it happened here," one Japanese official said after Ikeda's departure.
